Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: Māra, a 39-year-old park ranger of Māori descent, returned from a humanitarian mission in a war-torn region of the Middle East with a quiet, haunted silence that filled her days in the forest near her home. In the village of Al-Hawri, she had seen a child's arm ripped from a body, heard the shouts of soldiers as they swept through the street, and watched a makeshift medical tent collapse under a stray mortar. The memory of that night had never been fully stitched together; some moments were as clear as a sunrise over Lake Taupō, others were blank like a sheet left unattended. When she first came home, the smell of a perfume from a visiting aid worker-her own mother's favorite floral fragrance-brought the image of that child's tearful eyes back to the present, and a sudden, intrusive flash of the battle made her body tighten. That same day, Māra's reaction to the perfume, to the sudden motion of a passerby, and to the comforting embrace of a hug from her husband became the triggers that set off a cascade of avoidance. The scent of perfume made her want to leave the house, the quick movement of a stranger in the park made her dart away, and a hug from her spouse, which she had always found soothing, now felt like a threat, pushing her to avoid medical appointments, to skip visits to the local church, and to keep a guarded distance from anyone she met. The triggers did more than just prompt avoidance; they also pulled the fragments of her memory into a tangled net. Each scent or touch that awakened the war scene left her mind scrambling, a sudden rush of fear, and then the knowledge that she could not trace the narrative line. The flashbacks felt like a story that she could never fully retell, amplifying a sense of violation of her values-she had always believed in healing and kindness, but the war had shown her a darker, more brutal side of humanity. These negative appraisals amplified her sense that she had betrayed her own moral compass, that she no longer belonged anywhere, and that her life seemed devoid of meaning. Māra's sense that her values had been violated fed directly into her hypervigilance and the threat she felt whenever someone moved quickly or when she walked into an unfamiliar clearing in the park. The constant state of being on guard made her view each new place as a potential danger zone, and her belief that she had no place to belong only deepened this perception of threat. The hypervigilance also magnified the triggers she experienced; a sudden movement or a familiar scent felt more ominous, and her mind struggled to link these cues back to the disjointed memories of the war. These negative appraisals, in turn, pushed her further into avoidance: she stopped seeing a doctor when her skin began itching after a picnic, she turned away from her church when the doors opened, and she kept people at a distance on her walks through the forest. The threat that Māra felt-hypervigilance toward people, the sudden sense that a movement could be dangerous, and the need to avoid unfamiliar places-made her retreat even more. Her avoidance of the doctor's office meant that a skin condition could worsen, her avoidance of the church left her feeling spiritually adrift, and her avoidance of new locations kept her tethered to a narrow patch of the park, where she could see only what she had seen before. Each avoidance episode fed back into the threat she perceived; the less she confronted a new environment, the more it felt like a minefield. The threat also tightened the knot around her memories; each time she sidestepped an unfamiliar trail, her mind filled the blank space with fear, leaving the already fragmented story even more unclear. The fragmented memory of the war, the inability to weave a coherent narrative, further fed her avoidance. She could not explain the story to anyone, not even to herself; the moment she tried, she lost the thread and felt the familiar pull of panic. The incomplete story made it impossible to process, keeping her stuck in a cycle where each trigger pulled her deeper into withdrawal. Avoidance of medical care, religious spaces, and physical affection became her default coping mechanism; they provided a temporary sense of safety but, in the long run, only deepened her sense that she could not trust her own memory or find solace in familiar places. When Māra realized that her avoidance had begun to affect her work-she was missing patrols because she could not cross a stream she feared as potentially dangerous-and her marriage-her husband noticed she was less present during their evenings together-the urge to seek help became irresistible. She feared that if she continued to live in this loop of triggers, threat, memory, and negative appraisals, she might one day find herself unable to function at all. The most pressing hope she held is that a therapist could help her untangle the disjointed threads of her past so that she might regain the sense of belonging and meaning she once had, and that she might be able to step into the world again without feeling that every movement, scent, or touch was a potential flashback.
